comparator.name: Bachelor in Criminology
comparator.sourceNotes: The official 2026–2027 curriculum specifies a fixed 180-EC three-year bachelor: criminological and social-science foundations, legal study, two methods courses, three Research Lab stages, advanced criminology and criminal-law courses, a 15-EC minor, prevention and law-enforcement study, European justice, migration/diversity/crime, and a 15-EC analysis-and-reporting component. There are no formal bachelor routes requiring selection. The visible current table on brochure page 3 was inspected, rather than combining hidden older PDF text layers. The current study page corroborates Empirical legal studies (6 EC), Research Lab - de basis (7 EC), and the single 15-EC analysis/reporting component. The third-year skills strand combines the 6-EC application lab with the 15-EC analysis/reporting component; no extra thesis is added. The minor remains open and no formal route is imposed.
components: Open minor/exchange space in the third year.
European Law: Justice and Home Affairs

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Psychology, social behaviour and life-course development
Quantitative, qualitative and empirical criminological research
Crime prevention, public safety and policy evaluation
adjacent: Criminal justice, law, prevention and public safety
questions: Why does offending emerge and persist across people and social contexts?
How should law and public institutions prevent and respond to crime?

trace: provides a general economic framework for public intervention, externalities, efficiency and equity; it is not a specialist crime-policy or causal programme-evaluation course
provides research design, sampling, survey and statistical foundations for empirical criminological research
provides practical data cleaning, visualisation and analysis skills for working with empirical social-science data
provides foundational legal, socio-legal and normative perspectives on law, including criminal law and justice
adds human-rights law and rights-based reasoning relevant to criminal-justice institutions and sanctions

directly studies criminal accountability, guilt, defences, legality, punishment and criminal justice, including an introduction to interdisciplinary organised-crime research and a simulated legal-aid clinic
provides the international-law framework needed to understand cross-border legal cooperation and justice
examines constitutional and administrative limits on public authority, relevant to security governance and justice institutions
provides broad EU legal foundations in institutions, rights, citizenship and free movement; it is not a substitute for the specialised EU justice-and-home-affairs course
provides general moral theories and practical ethical reasoning for evaluating responsibility and justice; a dedicated penal-ethics syllabus is not claimed
provides concepts of justice, authority and political obligation for analysing the legitimacy of criminal-justice institutions
provides comparative institutional analysis for understanding how political systems organise public safety and policy responses
studies international-relations theories and interstate/security institutions; it complements the cross-border context rather than teaching criminal-justice cooperation
studies EU institutions, political power and policy-making, including a legislative research project; it does not establish specialist justice-and-home-affairs content
studies conflict, violence, peacebuilding and their structural and institutional contexts; this is an adjacent perspective, not a course in ordinary offending or a guaranteed radicalisation syllabus
introduces sociological concepts and theories for analysing the social causes and consequences of crime
provides qualitative research design, interviewing, interpretation and analysis skills relevant to criminological inquiry
develops sociological theory for explaining institutions, inequality and social change surrounding crime
adds advanced social theory on civil society, trust and solidarity relevant to social order and responses to crime
provides foundational psychological and behavioural science for evaluating individual-level explanations of offending
examines social influence, attitudes, groups and interpersonal behaviour relevant to offending, victimisation and social reactions
provides multivariate statistics and experimental methods for quantitative analysis of human behaviour
studies mental health and disorders through a biopsychosocial framework; it supplies psychological context without equating mental disorder with criminality or claiming forensic training
develops advanced evidence synthesis, meta-analysis and R-based research skills for evaluating empirical claims
studies development across the lifespan and provides a background perspective on age and behaviour; it does not itself teach criminal careers or repeat offending
examines youth radicalisation and evidence-based prevention, providing a concrete public-safety and prevention application

studies race, representation, systemic racism and US historical/media contexts including immigration enforcement; this is a specific exclusion/representation perspective, not a general crime-media or moral-panics course

alternatives.label: Crime, society & justice
alternatives.labelReason: The selected courses combine actual criminal-law/organised-crime study with substantial law, sociology, psychological science and empirical methods. The label describes related crime-and-justice inquiry without claiming a disciplinary criminology degree, victimology or specialist offender research.
alternatives.concept: Criminal responsibility and justice connect with sociology, social psychology and empirical research. Legal study, rights and social theory provide perspectives on crime and social responses, while developmental psychology and youth resilience offer specific behavioural and prevention-related contributions.
progression: Legal, sociological, political and behavioural foundations precede advanced criminal-law, social-theory, psychology and research work; the sociology sequence progresses from Introduction through Modern Sociology to advanced contemporary theory, and all formal prerequisites and term offerings are satisfied.

alternatives.label: Law, public authority & criminal justice
alternatives.labelReason: The institutional and normative emphasis is implemented by constitutional and criminal law, rights, political philosophy, EU politics, ethics and public economics. No dedicated public-safety planning or crime-policy evaluation sequence is claimed.
alternatives.concept: Criminal law, rights and constitutional study connect with political authority, ethics and European institutions. Sociology and empirical methods support the study of law and society, while public economics adds a general framework for assessing public intervention.
alternatives.distinctness: Political philosophy, EU politics, Public Economics and Ethics replace Abnormal Psychology, Lifespan Developmental Psychology, Advanced Research Seminar and Youth Resilience to Extremism. The four-course/30-EC difference shifts the organising inquiry from behavioural explanation and prevention applications toward public authority, institutional legality and normative judgment.
progression: Law and social-science foundations precede advanced criminal justice, EU politics, public economics and social theory; Research Methods & Statistics precedes Public Economics, and all formal prerequisites and term offerings are satisfied.

candidates.label: Law, public authority and criminal justice

selection.assessment: One additional evidenced institutional/legal direction is feasible and differs by four courses/30 EC. A separate victimisation/support direction was considered: human rights, social psychology and media/race supply particular perspectives but do not establish a materially distinct, sustained 24-course victimology/support programme from the current catalogue. No third option is manufactured. Crime-prevention interest 18 is assigned to the closest option, which actually includes the youth-resilience application; specialist crime-prevention and victimology limits remain explicit.

blocks: Brain & Behavior combines psychological and neuroscientific foundations. Its scope differs from the broad introductory psychology course.

Youth Resilience to Extremism studies a specific prevention application involving schools, civic engagement and psychosocial resilience. It does not cover the full criminological prevention-and-punishment syllabus.
Law, Society & Justice introduces legal, social and normative perspectives across several legal systems; it is not a Dutch-law course for criminologists.
The UCR course compares constitutional and administrative principles across legal systems; the Erasmus course focuses on the Dutch citizen-government legal relationship.
Shared criminal responsibility, legality and punishment themes support this relationship. UCR does not reproduce the Dutch introductory, procedural and substantive criminal-law sequence.
Broad EU-law foundations do not establish the specialised freedom, security and justice syllabus.

Statistics & Experimental Methods provides multivariate quantitative analysis. Erasmus Methods II also develops qualitative inquiry; the separate UCR qualitative course complements this partial relationship.
Systematic review, meta-analysis and R are not the same research process as the criminology-specific mixed-methods lab.

notes.text: Erasmus Criminology has a dedicated sequence in criminological theory, crime measurement and harm, criminal careers, Dutch criminal procedure/substantive law, law enforcement and mixed-methods research. UCR offers related socio-legal, psychological and empirical study, including actual criminal-law and organised-crime content, but does not reproduce that complete disciplinary sequence, specialised victimology/support training or the 21-EC final research strand. General EU law, psychology and evidence synthesis remain complementary perspectives.

audience.programmeDescription: Criminology at Erasmus University Rotterdam studies how crime is defined, explained and addressed, and how it affects people and society. The programme combines criminological theory, social science, law and empirical research.
audience.comparisonExplanation: Two UCR programmes offer related study through crime, society and justice, or through law and public authority. They combine criminal-law content with wider legal, social-science and research perspectives. Dedicated criminological theory, crime measurement, criminal careers, Dutch criminal procedure and the complete final research strand remain differences.

curriculum.limitation: The complete 180-EC curriculum includes a 15-EC open minor and a final research strand comprising Research Lab - de toepassing (6 EC) and Onderzoeksvaardigheden: analyse en rapportage (15 EC). No minor subject or specialisation is assumed.
